This file secures the material from the group phase for the essay (task 2.09).
For each meeting it records the content and my own contribution in two to three
sentences, so it can be used directly when planning the essay (task 5.01). Slides,
assignments and exports are stored outside the repository, since they contain data.

# Meetings

## Meeting 1 — 7 July 2026: Introduction

**Content.** Formal questions about the lab were clarified and the project was
presented in a short overview. As preparation we were asked to read one complete
issue of the Donnstags-Nachrichten, think about which aspects could be quantified,
and look at the Avisblatt project (Printed Markets, University of Basel).

**Own contribution.** I read the 1799 volume and summarised the first page of
advertisements, then derived five ideas for quantitative measures (price series,
market activity, seasonality, structural breaks, spatial distribution). I also
reviewed the Avisblatt pipeline and noted which of its design choices transfer to
our project (see [Preparation notes](#preparation-notes)).

## Meeting 2 — 17 July 2026: Digitisation pipeline and text line recognition

**Content.** After a short discussion of our close reading of one issue, the
digitisation pipeline was presented: visual segmentation of the pages and automatic
text line recognition. The first assignment was to create training material for the
text line recognition in Label Studio.

**Own contribution.** I corrected 20 text columns in Label Studio and sent the JSON
and COCO exports to Jakob Metzler by the 23 July deadline. I also raised two research
ideas: analysing *who* sells *what*, and a difference-in-differences design around the
Battle of Zurich (1799) based on the goods advertised.

## Meeting 3 — 20 July 2026: Large language models and generative AI

**Content.** Ways of using generative AI, training and test data, measuring success
rates, prompting, and cost. The assignment for the following week was to try out
text structuring with generative AI: splitting the recognised text of an issue into
section headers and individual advertisements and assigning each a category.

**Own contribution.** I ran the structuring fully locally with Ollama and compared
three strategies on a training sample of 5 issues and a held-out test sample of 10
issues of the Zürcher Wochenblatt (1801–1842, seed 20260710): (A) *direct*, one call
per issue with Gemma 4 12B (`gemma4:12b-it-qat`); (B) *verified*, rule-based
pre-segmentation where only uncertain sections and a final audit go to the same model;
and (C) *rules only*, the same pipeline without any model call. On the test sample,
strategy B performed best with an F1 of 0.84 for segmentation and category together,
against 0.47 for A and 0.67 for C; the monetary cost was zero, and the runtime about
19 minutes for 10 issues (B) compared with 29 minutes (A).

Own evaluation against the structured reference files of the course, at advertisement
level (a predicted advertisement counts as correct if its text matches a reference
advertisement with at least 90% similarity; "+ category" also requires the same
category):

| Strategy     | Sample    | Ads (ref. / pred.) | F1 segmentation | F1 + category | Model calls | Tokens in / out  | Runtime |
|--------------|-----------|-------------------:|----------------:|--------------:|------------:|-----------------:|--------:|
| A direct     | train (5) |          575 / 625 |            0.64 |          0.47 |           5 |  94,671 / 14,975 |  19 min |
| B verified   | train (5) |          575 / 592 |            0.87 |          0.87 |          22 |   87,516 / 9,180 |  13 min |
| C rules only | train (5) |          575 / 513 |            0.71 |          0.71 |           0 |                – |       – |
| A direct     | test (10) |          970 / 960 |            0.69 |          0.47 |          10 | 149,336 / 23,150 |  29 min |
| B verified   | test (10) |          970 / 958 |            0.84 |          0.84 |          40 | 134,316 / 13,447 |  19 min |
| C rules only | test (10) |          970 / 842 |            0.68 |          0.67 |           0 |                – |       – |

Settings: context window 32k tokens (A) and 16k (B), thinking off, output limit 8,192
(A) and 4,096 tokens (B). The table shows the second version of the prompts (v2); the
first version (v1, training sample only) gave practically the same values. The lesson
for the project: letting rules do the segmentation and using the model only where the
rules are uncertain is both more accurate and cheaper than handing the whole issue to
the model.

**Own contribution.** I took part in the session and noted the quanteda tutorials and

**Content.** The first half covered dating turning points with the Bry–Boschan

**Own contribution.** I took part in the session. Bry–Boschan dating and

# Preparation notes

## Reading a complete issue

I read the [1799 volume](https://www.e-rara.ch/zuz/content/titleinfo/16346607) on
e-rara. The first page of advertisements contains, in modern terms:

1. Extra-aged kirsch at 1 gulden 30 schilling and 2 gulden; only a few measures left, available at the "Kamel".
2. French liqueur and Mannheim water (a scented water) freshly arrived at Heinrich Notz, auf der Platte near Zurich; cheaper by the bottle, half dozen or dozen.
3. Leather shoes for women and children from Eberhard, shoemaker at the Augustinertor: women's shoes 1 gl. 30 s. to 2 gl. 18 s., children's shoes 38 s. to 1 gl. 28 s.
4. A wine press in good condition, suitable for about three to four harvests.
5. *Histoire universelle* (14 vols.) and *Histoire moderne* (22 vols.), quarto, new, with index; price and location from the Berichthaus.
6. A well-kept French horn with D-sharp and C crooks and mouthpieces, at a low price.
7. Good red potatoes from Waser, shoemaker in the Schmalzgrube.
8. Guinea fowl (or similar), various ornamental birds, one squirrel.
9. A felt boot and a pair of polished boots from Stolz in the Niederdorf, at the "Paradiesvogel".
10. White and dyed thread at various prices from Mrs Escher, Petershofstatt no. 160.
11. A men's fur coat covered with green camlet (wool cloth).
12. A long list of second-hand furniture, household goods and clothing from Joh. Heinrich Eichholzer, vordere Schipfe, "Wohlleben" (walnut chests and cupboards, chairs, mattresses, tables, an iron stove, cradles, copper kettles, sledges, spinning wheels, tea urns, waffle irons, men's and women's clothing), offered both for sale and as a buyer.
13. Red Burgundy wine at graded prices: 26 s. per bottle, 3 gl. 30 s. per half ohm, 7 gl. 8 s. per ohm, and quantity prices for 25, 50 and 100 bottles; at the "Weisse Kette" no. 220, vordere Schipfe.

### What can be measured?

1. **Price series of recurring, homogeneous goods.** Goods such as wine, grain,
   firewood, potatoes and oil probably appear weekly or at least regularly. This is
   the basis for a historical price index, built bottom-up from advertisements
   instead of official surveys, analogous to a CPI.
2. **Market activity as a frequency or volume signal.** Number of advertisements per
   issue, ratio of offers to requests, share of luxury versus basic goods, number of
   distinct sellers. This is essentially a diffusion index or activity measure, closer
   to an economic pulse than to prices.
3. **Seasonality.** With 52 issues per year, seasonal patterns (harvest-dependent
   goods, Christmas trade) can be estimated cleanly. This is needed anyway to separate
   the business cycle from the season.
4. **Structural breaks across years.** Wars, harvest failures and trade embargoes;
   with several volumes, regime changes can be identified.
5. **Spatial distribution.** If seller locations (Zurich, surrounding municipalities)
   are recorded, a spatial dimension can be added.

## The Avisblatt project

[Printed Markets](https://avisblatt.github.io/) (University of Basel, Department of
History, led by Prof. Susanna Burghartz, SNSF-funded 2019–2023) is a close analogue
to our project. It digitised the Basler Avisblatt (1729–1845), Switzerland's first
advertising newspaper: 118 volumes, 51,836 scanned pages and about 932,000 records of
advertisements and announcements.

### Pipeline

Source: [technical documentation](https://avisblatt.philhist.unibas.ch/media/uploads/files/Technical_documentation_Avisblatt-Project_Burghartz_et_al.pdf).

1. **Scanning** with a book scanner (Cobra A2); missing pages detected by comparing
   two redundant holdings (University Library and State Archives).
2. **Structuring in Freizo** (MongoDB-based) into the hierarchy volume → page →
   issue → advertisement. Issues were first marked manually in Mirador (header and date).
3. **Manual ground truth** for four volumes (1734, 1754, 1774, 1834): all
   advertisements segmented and classified by hand before training any automation.
   The key idea is not to annotate everything, but to annotate representative sample
   years completely and automate the rest.
4. **Handwritten text recognition in Transkribus** with two separate models for the
   18th and 19th centuries, since the typefaces changed; character error rate below 2%.
5. **Automatic segmentation** of advertisement boundaries with dhSegment, trained on
   the ground-truth boxes and corrected manually afterwards.
6. **Post-processing in R with quanteda:** dictionary- and regex-based tagging
   ("tagfilter"), named entity recognition for persons and places (Python, flair),
   language detection, and detection of duplicates and reprints.
7. **Publication** as open data via GitHub, Zenodo and CRAN, with a searchable web
   front end, following the FAIR principles.

### Relevance for our project

To select the ground-truth years, the team defined yearly dummy variables: a price
jump year (grain price at least 25% above the previous year), a price drop year (at
least 20% below), an abnormal price level (±25% / 20% from the seven-year mean), an
epidemic year, and a political or economic crisis year. The dummies ensured the
sample contained neither only normal nor only crisis years. This transfers to our
project in four ways:

- **Grain price as the lead indicator.** We could likewise choose one central price
  (bread, wine, potatoes) as an anchor series to calibrate business cycle swings.
- **Event dummies instead of full price indices.** A simpler but robust alternative
  to full index construction: set binary indicators for unusual periods per year or
  issue and regress advertising activity on them.
- **Stratified sampling instead of a full census.** With around 600 pages per year,
  digitise selected years or periods completely and sample in between; the selection
  logic (avoiding a sample that happens to hit only crisis years) carries over directly.
- **Reprint detection.** About three quarters of all advertisements were reprinted in
  the following issue. Without deduplication, an activity series based on advertisement
  counts would be biased upwards, overstating economic activity.
